questions.text: In this lesson, what does the European term “New World” refer to?
questions.answer: The Americas
choices: The Asian trading regions Europeans hoped to reach
The African ports used on routes toward Asia
The European kingdoms sponsoring ocean voyages
The Americas
questions.solution: Europeans used “New World” for the Americas. Indigenous peoples had lived there long before these European voyages.
questions.hint: Think about whose point of view made these lands seem “new.”
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

questions.text: Which instrument used the angle of the sun or stars to help sailors estimate latitude?
questions.answer: An astrolabe
choices: An astrolabe
A map showing coastlines and possible sailing routes
A ship’s log recording cargo and daily voyage events
A magnetic compass that indicated a ship’s heading
questions.solution: An astrolabe helped measure the angle of a visible heavenly body. Sailors could use that information to estimate latitude.
questions.hint: Latitude means position north or south of the equator.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: What did a magnetic compass mainly help a sailor determine?
questions.answer: Direction
choices: The number of miles remaining before reaching a port
The ship’s exact latitude and longitude together
Direction
The depth of water under the ship’s hull
questions.solution: A compass’s magnetic needle indicates north and helps a sailor keep a heading. It does not directly measure depth, age, or prices.
questions.hint: A compass answers “which way?”
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: What information is a navigation map designed to show?
questions.answer: Locations of land, water, and possible routes
choices: The personal motives of every sailor who followed a route
The amount of profit guaranteed by reaching each port
Locations of land, water, and possible routes
The exact weather at each point for every future voyage
questions.solution: Maps represent places and spatial relationships. They can help sailors plan routes and identify coasts or landing places.
questions.hint: A map represents where things are, rather than every fact about them.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

questions.text: In this lesson, what is a nation-state?
questions.answer: A country with its own government and territory
choices: A country with its own government and territory
A territory shared by all European rulers with no separate government
A trading ship that travels between several different countries
A community defined only by one cargo product rather than government
questions.solution: A nation-state has political authority over a territory. European rulers wanted to strengthen their countries through overseas expansion.
questions.hint: This word describes a political country, not an object on a ship.
questions.source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: Which belief system did many European missionaries seek to spread in the Americas?
questions.answer: Christianity
choices: Christianity
The belief that religion and European expansion were never connected
The belief that every Indigenous religion should remain unchanged
Religious beliefs they learned only after arriving in the Americas
questions.solution: European missionaries sought to spread Christianity. Religion was one motive for expansion, alongside wealth and political power.
questions.hint: Choose a religion, rather than a technology or economic activity.
questions.source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: Which pair of materials did European rulers value as precious metals?
questions.answer: Gold and silver
choices: Gold and tobacco sold as American crops
Silk and potatoes carried as food plants
Silver and spices used as navigation instruments
Gold and silver
questions.solution: Gold and silver were valued as wealth. Seeking them was an economic motive rather than a method of navigation.
questions.hint: Choose metals, rather than foods or ordinary construction materials.
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

questions.text: Which pair includes crops Indigenous peoples grew in the Americas before European arrival?
questions.answer: Corn and potatoes
choices: Wheat and barley introduced from Europe
Olives and wheat associated with the Mediterranean
Rice and tea associated with Asian agriculture
Corn and potatoes
questions.solution: Corn and potatoes were American crops that later spread widely beyond the Americas. Indigenous peoples cultivated them before European arrival.
questions.hint: Think of foods that traveled from the Americas to Europe.
questions.source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

questions.text: What is a cash crop?
questions.answer: A crop grown mainly to sell for income
choices: A crop defined by where it grows rather than its intended market
A crop grown mainly to sell for income
A crop grown mainly for the grower’s own household meals
A crop that can only be bought with gold rather than other goods
questions.solution: Cash crops are grown mainly for sale. The term describes the purpose of production, not a special kind of seed or coin-making plant.
questions.hint: Focus on why the grower is producing the crop.
questions.source: NPS: A Short History of Jamestown; Tobacco: Colonial Cultivation Methods

questions.text: What does an archaeologist study to learn about past people?
questions.answer: Artifacts, sites, and other physical evidence
choices: Only maps, without considering the people who made or used them
Only naturally occurring rocks unrelated to human activity
Only written accounts, without comparing them with physical remains
Artifacts, sites, and other physical evidence
questions.solution: Archaeologists study physical traces of past people and cultures. Objects and their locations can help answer historical questions.
questions.hint: Think about material evidence left by people.
questions.source: NPS: About Archeology; navigation, missions, and food references

questions.text: Why did many European merchants support voyages in the late 1400s?
questions.answer: They hoped to find profitable sea routes to Asian goods
choices: They hoped to find profitable sea routes to Asian goods
They wanted to avoid buying or selling goods abroad
They were certain a western sea route to Asia was already mapped
They wanted to bring Asian goods to the Americas without selling them
questions.solution: Demand for Asian goods, including spices and silk, encouraged the search for sea routes that could make trade more profitable.
questions.hint: Separate a reason for traveling from a tool used during travel.
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

questions.text: Far from shore, a sailor cannot see familiar hills or buildings. What navigation problem does this create?
questions.answer: Landmarks can no longer guide the ship’s position
choices: Magnetic north changes into the ship’s current latitude
The nearest coast must match every feature on the chart
Landmarks can no longer guide the ship’s position
Knowing the direction of travel gives an exact location
questions.solution: On the open ocean, familiar land features are missing. Sailors needed instruments, observations, and charts to navigate.
questions.hint: What kinds of clues disappear when land is out of sight?
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: The sky is cloudy and no stars are visible. Which tool can still help a sailor keep a direction?
questions.answer: A magnetic compass
choices: A cargo record showing the prices of the goods aboard
A magnetic compass
An astrolabe measuring the angle of a star hidden by clouds
A royal flag showing which country funded the voyage
questions.solution: A compass uses magnetism rather than a clear view of the stars. It remains useful when clouds block sky observations.
questions.hint: Choose the tool that does not need visible heavenly bodies.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: A returning sailor reports a coastline that earlier charts left out. What should a mapmaker do?
questions.answer: Compare the report with other evidence and revise the map if supported
choices: Compare the report with other evidence and revise the map if supported
Accept the report as proof that every older source is useless
Label the new coast as uninhabited simply because it was not mapped
Keep the chart unchanged because royal approval makes it accurate
questions.solution: New observations can improve maps, but comparing sources helps check accuracy. An early chart could be useful while still incomplete.
questions.hint: New evidence can improve a model without making every old detail wrong.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

questions.text: Why might an explorer carry a flag bearing a European ruler’s symbols?
questions.answer: To represent that ruler and make a claim to territory
choices: To measure latitude from the stars
To show that every Indigenous nation agreed with the claim
To prove that the land had no inhabitants
To represent that ruler and make a claim to territory
questions.solution: Flags could symbolize a ruler’s claimed authority. Raising one did not establish that existing inhabitants accepted the claim.
questions.hint: A flag can show who is making a claim without proving everyone accepts it.
questions.source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: Which shipboard object most directly suggests Christian religious activity?
questions.answer: A Bible
choices: An astrolabe used for observations during an ocean crossing
A written cargo list used to track the amount of silver
A Bible
A royal banner used to represent a European government
questions.solution: A Bible is a Christian religious text. Its presence can support a religious connection, although it cannot prove everyone aboard shared the same motive.
questions.hint: Look for an object used in religious teaching or worship.
questions.source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: Why could merchants profit from a new sea route to Asian spices?
questions.answer: They hoped to obtain valuable goods through more direct trade
choices: Merchants could profit only if Europeans had never wanted spices before
A new route would remove all costs and every risk from overseas trade
They hoped to obtain valuable goods through more direct trade
Asian goods would have no sale value once a sea route reached their source
questions.solution: European demand for Asian goods encouraged more direct trade routes. Merchants hoped sales would exceed the costs and risks of the voyages.
questions.hint: Connect demand for goods with the possibility of earning money.
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

questions.text: Which arrow correctly describes the later spread of American potatoes?
questions.answer: Americas → Europe
choices: Americas → Europe
Asia → Europe on Columbus’s 1492 return voyage
Europe → the Americas only after 1900
Europe → Americas before Indigenous farming
questions.solution: Potatoes were cultivated in the Americas before they were introduced to Europe. The arrow tracks the movement asked about, not all global exchange.
questions.hint: Start with the food’s origin, then identify the receiving region.
questions.source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

questions.text: Which crop native to the Americas became a major colonial export from Virginia to Europe?
questions.answer: Tobacco
choices: Olives originating in the Mediterranean region
Tea originating in Asia
Tobacco
Wheat originating outside the Americas
questions.solution: Tobacco became a profitable export from colonies such as Virginia to European markets. It is a classic cash-crop example.
questions.hint: Choose a crop grown for buyers rather than a metal or navigation tool.
questions.source: NPS: A Short History of Jamestown; Tobacco: Colonial Cultivation Methods

questions.solution: A compass helped sailors navigate. It was useful during travel rather than being a crop or a reason to seek converts.

The late 1400s

questions.text: Which pairing correctly distinguishes two navigation tools?

Astrolabe: compass direction; compass: latitude clues
Astrolabe: latitude clues; compass: direction
Astrolabe: sailing speed; compass: the sun’s height

questions.text: A map’s compass rose shows north at the top. Which direction is to the right?
questions.answer: East
choices: East
North
South
West
questions.solution: With north at the top of this compass rose, east is on the right, south at the bottom, and west on the left.
questions.hint: Use the order north, east, south, west around the compass rose.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: A teammate claims every European map in 1492 showed the Americas accurately. What is the best correction?
questions.answer: Maps reflected limited information and could contain errors

Trade with Asia meant European sailors had already charted every Atlantic island
Using a compass meant mapmakers could already draw all American coasts
Maps reflected limited information and could contain errors

questions.hint: A map can include only the information its makers have gathered or inferred.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

questions.text: Why did European rulers compete to claim land across the Atlantic?
questions.answer: Territory and resources could increase their power and wealth
choices: Territory and resources could increase their power and wealth
European claims meant Indigenous communities voluntarily changed rulers
Every ruler agreed that claiming land would end rivalry among countries
Claiming distant land meant rulers no longer needed trade or resources
questions.solution: Rulers sought resources, influence, and power. Competition among countries helped encourage exploration and colonization.
questions.hint: Think about what a ruler hoped their country would gain.
questions.source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: Why did Catholic rulers support priests traveling to the Americas?
questions.answer: They wanted to spread the Catholic Christian faith
choices: They wanted to spread the Catholic Christian faith
They expected missionaries to prevent every possible trading loss
They believed priests were needed mainly to draw more accurate coastlines
They wanted missionaries to make Indigenous beliefs the official religion in Europe
questions.solution: Supporting missionaries could serve a ruler’s religious goals. It was different from using instruments to navigate or searching for precious metals.
questions.hint: Connect a ruler’s religious support with conversion rather than location or cargo.
questions.source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: Which distinction correctly separates a motive from a tool?
questions.answer: Seeking silver is a motive; using an astrolabe is a method
choices: Carrying a royal flag always proves profit was the voyage’s only motive
Seeking silver is a motive; using an astrolabe is a method
Using a compass is a motive; earning trade profits is a navigation method
Seeking gold is a navigation tool; sailing a route is a religious goal
questions.solution: The wish to gain wealth explains why someone supports a voyage. An astrolabe helps explain how sailors navigate it.
questions.hint: Ask whether each item is a desired result or a way of traveling.
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

questions.text: Which cargo group contains American food plants rather than navigation tools?

choices: Silver cargo, a chart, and a magnetic compass
Corn, beans, and squash
Compass, astrolabe, and a hand-drawn sailing chart
Royal banner, Bible, and a written proclamation
questions.solution: Corn, beans, and squash are food crops with Indigenous American histories. The other lists include instruments, symbols, or metals.
questions.hint: Separate things people grew and ate from objects used to sail.
questions.source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

questions.text: Farmer A grows beans mainly for family meals. Farmer B grows tobacco mainly to sell abroad. Which is the cash-crop example?
questions.answer: Farmer B’s tobacco
choices: Only Farmer A’s beans
Both, because every plant is always a cash crop
Neither, because crops cannot be sold
Farmer B’s tobacco
questions.solution: The described purpose matters. Farmer B grows tobacco chiefly for sale; Farmer A’s beans are primarily for the household to eat.
questions.hint: Look for the crop intended mainly for a market.
questions.source: NPS: A Short History of Jamestown; Tobacco: Colonial Cultivation Methods

questions.text: Which matching set correctly connects three objects with lesson categories?
questions.answer: Astrolabe → navigation; royal flag → claimed power; tobacco → product
choices: Astrolabe → food; royal flag → latitude; tobacco → direction
Astrolabe → gold; royal flag → food; tobacco → navigation
Astrolabe → navigation; royal flag → claimed power; tobacco → product
Astrolabe → religion; royal flag → crop; tobacco → map
questions.solution: These matches use each object’s historical function: an instrument, a political symbol, and a crop for trade.

questions.text: Columbus sailed west across the Atlantic in 1492 hoping to reach which trading region?
questions.answer: Asia
choices: The English colonies that already existed on the Atlantic coast
The gold mines of Mexico that he had previously visited
Asia
The Americas, which he already knew were between Europe and Asia
questions.solution: Columbus hoped to reach Asia by sailing west for Spain. He reached islands in the Americas instead.
questions.hint: Distinguish the destination he hoped for from the place he actually reached.
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

questions.text: A squadmate says an astrolabe instantly showed a ship’s exact location on a screen. What is the best correction?
questions.answer: It measured sky angles to help estimate latitude, not a screen location
choices: It pointed toward magnetic north so sailors could steer a heading
It automatically drew coastlines that sailors had not yet visited
It gave exact east–west position without needing sky observations
It measured sky angles to help estimate latitude, not a screen location
questions.solution: An astrolabe was an observing instrument, not an electronic location system. Position estimates required observations and calculations.
questions.hint: Think of observing the sky rather than receiving a satellite signal.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: A navigator knows the ship is heading west. What can a compass alone NOT tell the navigator?
questions.answer: The ship’s exact location in the ocean
choices: A reference direction for north
The direction opposite east
Whether the heading is generally west
The ship’s exact location in the ocean
questions.solution: Knowing a direction is not the same as knowing a location. A compass provides a heading reference, not an exact position.
questions.hint: Many ships can face west while being in very different places.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

questions.text: A sketch map has a harbor west of an island. With north at the top, where is the harbor?
questions.answer: To the left of the island
choices: To the left of the island
To the right of the island
Directly above the island
Directly below the island
questions.solution: When north is at the top, west is to the left. The compass rose supplies the needed orientation.
questions.hint: Use the map’s stated orientation, not a guess about a real coast.
questions.source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

questions.text: A European journal calls a place “newly discovered,” but Indigenous families already live there. Which statement includes both perspectives?
questions.answer: It was new to those visitors, not a place without history or people
choices: A journal’s claim establishes Indigenous agreement with European control
It was new to those visitors, not a place without history or people
A European name erased the names and histories already used by local people
The families’ presence meant no European could ever be unfamiliar with the place
questions.solution: A European visitor’s description reflects that visitor’s knowledge. Indigenous peoples already had their own homes, names, histories, and political communities.
questions.hint: Ask “new to whom?” before accepting a discovery claim.
questions.source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

questions.text: An archaeologist finds one Bible in a shipwreck. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.answer: Christian religious materials were carried on that ship
choices: Every person aboard traveled only for religion
Every Indigenous person accepted the visitors’ religion
The ship could not have carried trade goods
Christian religious materials were carried on that ship
questions.solution: The artifact supports the presence of Christian materials. One object cannot establish every traveler’s belief or rule out other purposes.
questions.hint: Make the smallest claim supported by the evidence you have.
questions.source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

question.text: Why did European rulers compete to claim land across the Atlantic?
question.answer: Territory and resources could increase their power and wealth
choices: Territory and resources could increase their power and wealth
European claims meant Indigenous communities voluntarily changed rulers
Every ruler agreed that claiming land would end rivalry among countries
Claiming distant land meant rulers no longer needed trade or resources
question.solution: Rulers sought resources, influence, and power. Competition among countries helped encourage exploration and colonization.
question.hint: Think about what a ruler hoped their country would gain.
question.source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

answers: Territory and resources could increase their power and wealth

question.text: Why did Catholic rulers support priests traveling to the Americas?
question.answer: They wanted to spread the Catholic Christian faith
choices: They wanted to spread the Catholic Christian faith
They expected missionaries to prevent every possible trading loss
They believed priests were needed mainly to draw more accurate coastlines
They wanted missionaries to make Indigenous beliefs the official religion in Europe
question.solution: Supporting missionaries could serve a ruler’s religious goals. It was different from using instruments to navigate or searching for precious metals.
question.hint: Connect a ruler’s religious support with conversion rather than location or cargo.
question.source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

answers: They wanted to spread the Catholic Christian faith

question.text: Which distinction correctly separates a motive from a tool?
question.answer: Seeking silver is a motive; using an astrolabe is a method
choices: Carrying a royal flag always proves profit was the voyage’s only motive
Seeking silver is a motive; using an astrolabe is a method
Using a compass is a motive; earning trade profits is a navigation method
Seeking gold is a navigation tool; sailing a route is a religious goal
question.solution: The wish to gain wealth explains why someone supports a voyage. An astrolabe helps explain how sailors navigate it.
question.hint: Ask whether each item is a desired result or a way of traveling.
question.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

answers: Seeking silver is a motive; using an astrolabe is a method

question.text: Which cargo group contains American food plants rather than navigation tools?
question.answer: Corn, beans, and squash
choices: Silver cargo, a chart, and a magnetic compass
Corn, beans, and squash
Compass, astrolabe, and a hand-drawn sailing chart
Royal banner, Bible, and a written proclamation
question.solution: Corn, beans, and squash are food crops with Indigenous American histories. The other lists include instruments, symbols, or metals.
question.hint: Separate things people grew and ate from objects used to sail.
question.source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

answers: Corn, beans, and squash

question.text: Farmer A grows beans mainly for family meals. Farmer B grows tobacco mainly to sell abroad. Which is the cash-crop example?
question.answer: Farmer B’s tobacco
choices: Only Farmer A’s beans
Both, because every plant is always a cash crop
Neither, because crops cannot be sold
Farmer B’s tobacco
question.solution: The described purpose matters. Farmer B grows tobacco chiefly for sale; Farmer A’s beans are primarily for the household to eat.
question.hint: Look for the crop intended mainly for a market.
question.source: NPS: A Short History of Jamestown; Tobacco: Colonial Cultivation Methods

answers: Farmer B’s tobacco

question.text: Which matching set correctly connects three objects with lesson categories?
question.answer: Astrolabe → navigation; royal flag → claimed power; tobacco → product
choices: Astrolabe → food; royal flag → latitude; tobacco → direction
Astrolabe → gold; royal flag → food; tobacco → navigation
Astrolabe → navigation; royal flag → claimed power; tobacco → product
Astrolabe → religion; royal flag → crop; tobacco → map
question.solution: These matches use each object’s historical function: an instrument, a political symbol, and a crop for trade.
question.hint: Use tools for how, symbols for motives, and cargo for products.
question.source: NPS: About Archeology; navigation, missions, and food references

answers: Astrolabe → navigation; royal flag → claimed power; tobacco → product

questions.text: A merchant funds a voyage hoping to sell its cargo for more than the voyage costs. What is the main motive?
questions.answer: Profit
choices: Profit
Recording the locations of unfamiliar coastlines
Converting people to a religious faith
Measuring the ship’s latitude from the stars
questions.solution: The merchant expects a financial gain from trade. That is an economic motive, even if others on the voyage have additional goals.
questions.hint: Follow what this particular merchant hopes to gain.
questions.source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

questions.text: A label says, “Europeans invented corn when they found the Americas.” Which correction is accurate?
questions.answer: Indigenous peoples had cultivated corn long before European arrival
choices: Indigenous people began farming only after European explorers arrived
Corn was developed in Europe and first carried west by Columbus
Indigenous peoples had cultivated corn long before European arrival
European maps are the only evidence that a crop existed before contact
questions.solution: American crops were the result of Indigenous agricultural knowledge and cultivation. European arrival helped spread them abroad, not invent them.
questions.hint: Distinguish growing and developing a crop from carrying it somewhere new.
questions.source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

questions.text: In 2.200, what is the value of the digit 2 in the tenths place?
questions.solution: The tenths place is 1 place to the right of the decimal point. 2 tenths = 0.2.
questions.hint: Name each place as you move right from the decimal point.

questions.text: Fill in the equivalent decimal: 2.5 = ___ (write three decimal places).
questions.solution: 2.5 = 2.500. Trailing zeros do not change the value.
questions.hint: Zeros at the end of the decimal part do not change its value.

question.text: In 2.200, what is the value of the digit 2 in the tenths place?

question.hint: Name each place as you move right from the decimal point.

questions.text: Calculate 1.2 × 2.
questions.solution: 1.2 × 2 = 2.4. Multiply 12 × 2 = 24; the factors have 1 decimal places in all. Divide that whole-number product by 10 and keep all places.
questions.hint: Think of equal groups. Multiply the digits and preserve the value of each decimal place.
questions.source: Provisional family-approved scope; 5.NBT.B.7. Chapter 4 contents unverified.

questions.text: Calculate 2.5 × 0.3.
questions.solution: 2.5 × 0.3 = 0.75. Multiply 25 × 03 = 75; the factors have 2 decimal places in all. Divide that whole-number product by 100 and keep all places.
questions.hint: Tenths times tenths give hundredths. Count places in both factors, then check the size.
questions.source: Provisional family-approved scope; 5.NBT.B.7. Chapter 4 contents unverified.

questions.text: A squad pours sand and steel paperclips into one supply tray. Why is this a mixture?
questions.answer: Two substances are combined and keep their original properties
choices: Two substances are combined and keep their original properties
The sand changes into steel
Every combination forms a new substance
The paperclips lose their magnetism
questions.solution: The sand is still sand, and the steel paperclips still have their own properties. Combining materials can make a mixture without a chemical change.
questions.hint: Ask whether the original materials keep their own properties.
